name: Cosmic Latte
lede: Cosmic latte is a warm off-white, the name two astronomers gave to the average color of the light of the universe.

sections.title: The color of the universe
sections.body:
In a survey of the light from over 200,000 galaxies, two scientists worked out what the universe would look like if all its light could be seen at once [1][2]. The answer was beige [2]. They tried names such as "big bang buff" and "skyvory", then settled on *cosmic latte* [2].

The first announcement, in January 2002, said the universe was turquoise [1]. Three months later Johns Hopkins University corrected it: the turquoise was a computer bug, and the true color is off-white, like house paint [1]. The co-author Karl Glazebrook said the result was meant as an amusing footnote to the survey, and that it was his favorite tag [1]. The turquoise universe is a myth to unlearn.

The swatch here, #FFF8E7, is the one cited by Wikipedia from Glazebrook and Baldry [3]. Its closest named neighbor is [[ivory]], at a CIEDE2000 distance of 3.4 [3]. St Clair uses the story to illustrate beige's image problem, as a color chiefly used as a foil [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: As a painted color, cosmic latte is common: it appears in 385 of 23,781 paintings in our archive and is more common than 72% of the named colors [4]. It most often plays a light (62% of 224 paintings) [4]. It is over-represented in Chinese painting, at 3.9 times the expected rate (40 of 635 paintings) [4]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [4].

questions.q: What was the first, mistaken color announced for the universe?
What was the true result of the survey?
True or false: the first turquoise announcement turned out to be right.

openers: The universe was announced as turquoise in 2002; a computer bug, and three months later it was corrected to beige.
